# slide10
int Type Size Specifiers
Specifying the size of an int ensures that the type contains a minimum number of bits. The three specifiers are:
short: at least 16 bits
long: at least 32 bits
long long: at least 64 bits
Standard C does not specify that a long double must occupy a minimum number of bits, only that it occupies no fewer bits than a double.

const Qualifier
Any type can hold a constant value.
A constant value cannot be changed.
To qualify a type as holding a constant value we use the keyword const
A type qualified as const is unmodifiable.
If a program instruction attempts to modify a const qualified type, the compiler will report an error.

# slide16
Negative and Positive Values
Computers store negative integers using encoding schemes:
Two's complement notation,
One's complement notation, and
Sign magnitude notation.
All of these schemes represent non-negative integers identically.
The most popular scheme is two's complement.
To obtain the two's complement of an integer, we:
Flip the bits (1-complement)
Add one  2-complement

6. Mixing Data Types
Although the ALU does not perform operations on operands of differing data type directly, C compilers can interpret expressions that contain operands of differing data type.
If a binary expression contains operands of differing type, a C compiler changes the data type of one of the operands to match the other.
Data type hierarchy: double, float, long, int , char .

# slide58
6. Mixing Data Types (cont.)
Implicit Casting for the assignment
If the data type of the variable on the left side of an assignment operator differs from the data type of the right side operand, the compiler:
Promotes the right operand to the data type of the left operand if the left operand is of a higher data type than the right operand,
Truncates the right operand to the data type of the left operand if the left operand is of a lower data type than the right operand.

Questions.Title: Choosing a data type for a book ID
Questions.Description: A program needs to store a unique book ID such as 2345678901. Which data type is the most suitable choice among the options below?
Questions.Explanation: The best choice is int because the chunks state that int stores integer values, while char is for small integers or single characters and float/double are for floating-point numbers. A book ID like 2345678901 is an integer value, so int is the most appropriate among the given options. char is too small for such a large ID, and float/double are not the right kinds of types for exact integral identifiers.

Questions.Title: Valid C variable name
Questions.Description: Which of the following is a valid C variable name based on the naming rules?
Questions.Explanation: total_books is valid because names can contain letters, digits, and underscores, must begin with a letter or underscore, must not contain whitespace or special characters, and must not be a C reserved word. 2totalBooks is invalid because it begins with a digit. total books is invalid because it contains a space. int is invalid because it is a reserved word.

Output.Title: Choosing a suitable data type for a large book ID
Output.Description: A program needs to store the unique ID of a book such as 2345678901. Which data type is the most suitable choice among the options below?
Output.Explanation: An integer ID like 2345678901 should be stored with an integral type. The chunks state that int is used for integer values, while char is for small integers or single characters, and float/double are floating-point types for real numbers. Among the given choices, int is the most suitable match. Float and double are not intended for exact integer IDs, and char is far too small.

Output.Title: Valid C variable name
Output.Description: Which of the following is a valid C variable name based on the naming rules?
Output.Explanation: A valid name may contain letters, digits, and underscores, must begin with a letter or underscore, must not contain whitespaces or special characters, and must not be a reserved word. total_books follows these rules. 2totalBooks starts with a digit, total books contains a space, and int is a reserved word.

Output.Title: Effect of modifying a const-qualified value
Output.Description: What happens if a program instruction attempts to modify a value declared with the const qualifier?
Options: A. The value changes normally at runtime.
B. The compiler reports an error.
C. The value becomes unsigned automatically.
D. The compiler allocates no memory for the variable.
Output.Explanation: The chunks state that a const-qualified type is unmodifiable, and if a program instruction attempts to modify it, the compiler reports an error. The other options do not match that rule: const does not make a value change normally, does not automatically change signedness, and the memory-allocation statement belongs to #define macros, not const.

Output.Title: Meaning of arguments in scanf
Output.Description: In the call scanf("%d%d", &n, &m), what do the two ampersands before n and m indicate?
Options: A. They pass the addresses of n and m so the input values can be stored there.
B. They convert the integers into floating-point values.
C. They print n and m to the screen before reading input.
D. They mean scanf will only accept blank keys, not Enter.
Output.Explanation: The chunks explain that scanf receives data holders and stores the converted input into memory locations, and that & gets the address of a variable. Therefore, &n and &m pass the addresses of the variables so scanf can write the input values into them. The other options are incorrect: & is not for conversion or printing, and scanf accepts blank or Enter as separators.

Output.Title: Tracing an arithmetic expression with division
Output.Description: Given the expression 10.0 / 3, what result is shown by the examples in the provided material?
Options: D. Error because division cannot use decimal numbers
Output.Explanation: The arithmetic operator examples show that 10/3 gives 3, while 10.0/3 gives 3.3333333. Since 10.0 is a floating-point value, the division is performed in floating-point form and produces a non-integer result. The other choices do not match the demonstrated behavior.

questions.Title: Choosing a suitable data type for a large book ID
questions.Description: A program needs to store the unique ID of a book such as 2345678901. Which data type is the most suitable choice among the options below?
questions.Explanation: An integer ID like 2345678901 should be stored with an integral type. The chunks state that int is used for integer values, while char is for small integers or single characters, and float/double are floating-point types for real numbers. Among the given choices, int is the most suitable match. Float and double are not intended for exact integer IDs, and char is far too small.

questions.Title: Valid C variable name
questions.Description: Which of the following is a valid C variable name based on the naming rules?
questions.Explanation: A valid name may contain letters, digits, and underscores, must begin with a letter or underscore, must not contain whitespaces or special characters, and must not be a reserved word. total_books follows these rules. 2totalBooks starts with a digit, total books contains a space, and int is a reserved word.

questions.Title: Effect of modifying a const-qualified value
questions.Description: What happens if a program instruction attempts to modify a value declared with the const qualifier?
Options: A. The value changes normally at runtime.
B. The compiler reports an error.
C. The value becomes unsigned automatically.
D. The compiler allocates no memory for the variable.
questions.Explanation: The chunks state that a const-qualified type is unmodifiable, and if a program instruction attempts to modify it, the compiler reports an error. The other options do not match that rule: const does not make a value change normally, does not automatically change signedness, and the memory-allocation statement belongs to #define macros, not const.

questions.Title: Meaning of arguments in scanf
questions.Description: In the call scanf("%d%d", &n, &m), what do the two ampersands before n and m indicate?
Options: A. They pass the addresses of n and m so the input values can be stored there.
B. They convert the integers into floating-point values.
C. They print n and m to the screen before reading input.
D. They mean scanf will only accept blank keys, not Enter.
questions.Explanation: The chunks explain that scanf receives data holders and stores the converted input into memory locations, and that & gets the address of a variable. Therefore, &n and &m pass the addresses of the variables so scanf can write the input values into them. The other options are incorrect: & is not for conversion or printing, and scanf accepts blank or Enter as separators.

questions.Title: Choosing a suitable data type for a large book ID
questions.Description: A program needs to store the unique ID of a book such as 2345678901. Which data type is the most suitable choice among the options below?
questions.Explanation: An integer ID like 2345678901 should be stored with an integral type. The chunks state that int is used for integer values, while char is for small integers or single characters, and float/double are floating-point types for real numbers. Among the given choices, int is the most suitable match. Float and double are not intended for exact integer IDs, and char is far too small.

questions.Title: Valid C variable name
questions.Description: Which of the following is a valid C variable name based on the naming rules?
questions.Explanation: A valid name may contain letters, digits, and underscores, must begin with a letter or underscore, must not contain whitespaces or special characters, and must not be a reserved word. total_books follows these rules. 2totalBooks starts with a digit, total books contains a space, and int is a reserved word.

questions.Title: Effect of modifying a const-qualified value
questions.Description: What happens if a program instruction attempts to modify a value declared with the const qualifier?
Options: A. The value changes normally at runtime.
B. The compiler reports an error.
C. The value becomes unsigned automatically.
D. The compiler allocates no memory for the variable.
questions.Explanation: The chunks state that a const-qualified type is unmodifiable, and if a program instruction attempts to modify it, the compiler reports an error. The other options do not match that rule: const does not make a value change normally, does not automatically change signedness, and the memory-allocation statement belongs to #define macros, not const.

questions.Title: Meaning of arguments in scanf
questions.Description: In the call scanf("%d%d", &n, &m), what do the two ampersands before n and m indicate?
Options: A. They pass the addresses of n and m so the input values can be stored there.
B. They convert the integers into floating-point values.
C. They print n and m to the screen before reading input.
D. They mean scanf will only accept blank keys, not Enter.
questions.Explanation: The chunks explain that scanf receives data holders and stores the converted input into memory locations, and that & gets the address of a variable. Therefore, &n and &m pass the addresses of the variables so scanf can write the input values into them. The other options are incorrect: & is not for conversion or printing, and scanf accepts blank or Enter as separators.

questions.Title: Tracing an arithmetic expression with division
questions.Description: Given the expression 10.0 / 3, what result is shown by the examples in the provided material?
Options: D. Error because division cannot use decimal numbers
questions.Explanation: The arithmetic operator examples show that 10/3 gives 3, while 10.0/3 gives 3.3333333. Since 10.0 is a floating-point value, the division is performed in floating-point form and produces a non-integer result. The other choices do not match the demonstrated behavior.

int Type Size Specifiers
Specifying the size of an int ensures that the type contains a minimum number of bits. The three specifiers are:
short: at least 16 bits
long: at least 32 bits
long long: at least 64 bits
Standard C does not specify that a long double must occupy a minimum number of bits, only that it occupies no fewer bits than a double.

Although the ALU does not perform operations on operands of differing data type directly, C compilers can interpret expressions that contain operands of differing data type.
If a binary expression contains operands of differing type, a C compiler changes the data type of one of the operands to match the other.

Implicit Casting for the assignment
If the data type of the variable on the left side of an assignment operator differs from the data type of the right side operand, the compiler:
Promotes the right operand to the data type of the left operand if the left operand is of a higher data type than the right operand,
Truncates the right operand to the data type of the left operand if the left operand is of a lower data type than the right operand.

# slide10
int Type Size Specifiers
Specifying the size of an int ensures that the type contains a minimum number of bits. The three specifiers are:
short: at least 16 bits
long: at least 32 bits
long long: at least 64 bits
Standard C does not specify that a long double must occupy a minimum number of bits, only that it occupies no fewer bits than a double.

double Type Size Specifier
The size of a long double depends on the environment and is typically at least 64 bits:
long double type only ensures that it contains at least as many bits as a double

const Qualifier
Any type can hold a constant value.
A constant value cannot be changed.
To qualify a type as holding a constant value we use the keyword const
A type qualified as const is unmodifiable.
If a program instruction attempts to modify a const qualified type, the compiler will report an error.

Representing Values
Hardware manufacturers distinguish integral types from floating-point types and represent integral data and floating-point data differently.
Integral types: char, int
Floating-point types: float, double

# slide14
Representation of Integral Values
C stores integral values in equivalent binary form.
Non-Negative Values:
Intel uses this little-endian ordering.
Motorola uses big-endian ordering.

Value is stored:
09F5E103
Least significant is stored in lowest byte

Each CPU family has it’s own way to store data . So, compilers must have a suitable way for copying data from this variable to other. And due to this reason also, each compiler can run well only on a specific family of CPU only. A supplier may supply some versions of their compiler for some CPU families.

Negative and Positive Values
Computers store negative integers using encoding schemes:
Two's complement notation,
One's complement notation, and
Sign magnitude notation.
All of these schemes represent non-negative integers identically.
The most popular scheme is two's complement.
To obtain the two's complement of an integer, we:
Flip the bits (1-complement)
Add one  2-complement

questions.Title: Choosing a data type for a book ID
questions.Description: A program needs to store a unique book ID such as 2345678901. Which data type is the most suitable choice among the options below?
questions.Explanation: The best choice is int because the chunks state that int stores integer values, while char is for small integers or single characters and float/double are for floating-point numbers. A book ID like 2345678901 is an integer value, so int is the most appropriate among the given options. char is too small for such a large ID, and float/double are not the right kinds of types for exact integral identifiers.

questions.Title: Valid C variable name
questions.Description: Which of the following is a valid C variable name based on the naming rules?
questions.Explanation: total_books is valid because names can contain letters, digits, and underscores, must begin with a letter or underscore, must not contain whitespace or special characters, and must not be a C reserved word. 2totalBooks is invalid because it begins with a digit. total books is invalid because it contains a space. int is invalid because it is a reserved word.

questions.Title: Attempting to modify a const-qualified value
questions.Description: What happens if a program instruction attempts to modify a value declared with the const qualifier?
Options: A. The value changes normally at runtime.
B. The compiler reports an error.
C. The value becomes unsigned automatically.
D. The variable is converted into a macro.
questions.Explanation: A const-qualified type is unmodifiable. The chunk explicitly says that if a program instruction attempts to modify a const qualified type, the compiler will report an error. The value does not change normally, it does not become unsigned, and const is not the same as a macro replacement created by #define.

questions.Title: Meaning of addresses in scanf
questions.Description: In the call scanf("%d%d", &n, &m), what do the two ampersands before n and m indicate?
Options: A. They pass the addresses of n and m so the input values can be stored there.
B. They convert the input values into floating-point numbers.
C. They print n and m before reading input.
D. They tell scanf to ignore Enter and only accept letters.
questions.Explanation: The chunk explains that scanf receives data holders and stores converted input into memory locations, and that & gets the address of a variable. Therefore, &n and &m pass the addresses of those variables so scanf can store the input values there. The other choices are incorrect: & does not perform type conversion, printing, or input filtering.

questions.Title: Result of floating-point division
questions.Description: Given the expression 10.0 / 3, what result is shown by the examples in the provided material?
Options: D. Error because division cannot use decimal numbers
questions.Explanation: The arithmetic operator example states that 10/3 gives 3, while 10.0/3 gives 3.3333333. Because 10.0 is a floating-point value, the division is performed in floating-point form and produces a non-integer result. The other options do not match the demonstrated behavior.

# slide10
int Type Size Specifiers
Specifying the size of an int ensures that the type contains a minimum number of bits. The three specifiers are:
short: at least 16 bits
long: at least 32 bits
long long: at least 64 bits
Standard C does not specify that a long double must occupy a minimum number of bits, only that it occupies no fewer bits than a double.

long double type only ensures that it contains at least as many bits as a double

const Qualifier
Any type can hold a constant value.
A constant value cannot be changed.
To qualify a type as holding a constant value we use the keyword const
A type qualified as const is unmodifiable.
If a program instruction attempts to modify a const qualified type, the compiler will report an error.

Hardware manufacturers distinguish integral types from floating-point types and represent integral data and floating-point data differently.
Integral types: char, int
Floating-point types: float, double

C stores integral values in equivalent binary form.
Non-Negative Values:
Intel uses this little-endian ordering.
Motorola uses big-endian ordering.

Negative and Positive Values
Computers store negative integers using encoding schemes:
Two's complement notation,
One's complement notation, and
Sign magnitude notation.
All of these schemes represent non-negative integers identically.
The most popular scheme is two's complement.
To obtain the two's complement of an integer, we:
Flip the bits (1-complement)
Add one  2-complement

6. Mixing Data Types (cont.)
Implicit Casting for the assignment
If the data type of the variable on the left side of an assignment operator differs from the data type of the right side operand, the compiler:
Promotes the right operand to the data type of the left operand if the left operand is of a higher data type than the right operand,
Truncates the right operand to the data type of the left operand if the left operand is of a lower data type than the right operand.

questions.Title: Choosing a data type for a book ID
questions.Description: A program needs to store a unique book ID such as 2345678901. Which data type is the most suitable choice among the options below?
questions.Explanation: The best choice is int because the chunks state that int stores integer values, while char is for small integers or single characters and float/double are for floating-point numbers. A book ID like 2345678901 is an integer value, so int is the most appropriate among the given options. char is too small for such a large ID, and float/double are not the right kinds of types for exact integral identifiers.

questions.Title: Valid C variable name
questions.Description: Which of the following is a valid C variable name based on the naming rules?
questions.Explanation: total_books is valid because names can contain letters, digits, and underscores, must begin with a letter or underscore, must not contain whitespace or special characters, and must not be a C reserved word. 2totalBooks is invalid because it begins with a digit. total books is invalid because it contains a space. int is invalid because it is a reserved word.

questions.Title: Attempting to modify a const-qualified value
questions.Description: What happens if a program instruction attempts to modify a value declared with the const qualifier?
Options: A. The value changes normally at runtime.
B. The compiler reports an error.
C. The value becomes unsigned automatically.
D. The variable is converted into a macro.
questions.Explanation: A const-qualified type is unmodifiable. The chunk explicitly says that if a program instruction attempts to modify a const qualified type, the compiler will report an error. The value does not change normally, it does not become unsigned, and const is not the same as a macro replacement created by #define.

questions.Title: Meaning of addresses in scanf
questions.Description: In the call scanf("%d%d", &n, &m), what do the two ampersands before n and m indicate?
Options: A. They pass the addresses of n and m so the input values can be stored there.
B. They convert the input values into floating-point numbers.
C. They print n and m before reading input.
D. They tell scanf to ignore Enter and only accept letters.
questions.Explanation: The chunk explains that scanf receives data holders and stores converted input into memory locations, and that & gets the address of a variable. Therefore, &n and &m pass the addresses of those variables so scanf can store the input values there. The other choices are incorrect: & does not perform type conversion, printing, or input filtering.

questions.Title: Result of floating-point division
questions.Description: Given the expression 10.0 / 3, what result is shown by the examples in the provided material?
Options: D. Error because division cannot use decimal numbers
questions.Explanation: The arithmetic operator example states that 10/3 gives 3, while 10.0/3 gives 3.3333333. Because 10.0 is a floating-point value, the division is performed in floating-point form and produces a non-integer result. The other options do not match the demonstrated behavior.

rubric.title: C Programming Fundamentals - Multiple Choice Rubric

institution_context.target_students: FPT University students in foundational programming courses
course_context: Beginner-friendly assessment tone with academic rigor

easy.description: Single-concept recall or direct interpretation questions about basic C syntax or semantics.
expected_skills: Identify variable, data type, operator, or control-flow behavior.
Recognize simple array, loop, function, or pointer basics.
Answer without multi-step tracing or deep debugging.

medium.description: Questions requiring short reasoning chains, code tracing, or understanding of common mistakes in beginner C programs.
expected_skills: Trace loops, arrays, or function calls.
Reason about pointer usage at a basic to intermediate level.
Detect common semantic mistakes or output behavior.
should_avoid: Advanced undefined behavior traps that are not grounded in the source material.

hard.description: Questions requiring careful code tracing, deeper semantic understanding, or subtle reasoning about pointers, arrays, functions, or memory behavior.
expected_skills: Differentiate close distractors based on true C semantics.
Reason about non-trivial pointer or array behavior if grounded in the chunks.
should_avoid: Topics not present in introductory C course material.

review_checks: The question must be grounded in the provided chunks.
The requested difficulty must match the actual reasoning demand.
Options must be plausible, non-duplicate, and clearly distinguishable.
correct_answer must match valid option labels.
Explanation must justify the correct answer using C fundamentals.
The question must stay within introductory C scope.

easy: Requires multi-step tracing across several statements or functions.
Uses tricky pointer semantics that exceed beginner recall.
Includes distractors that require advanced edge-case knowledge.
medium: Can be answered by direct definition recall only.
Depends on content absent from the chunks.
hard: Only tests a single factual definition.
Does not require meaningful reasoning beyond beginner recall.

acceptance_rules: Accept only if schema is valid, content is grounded, and difficulty is aligned.
Reject if the question exceeds introductory C scope without chunk support.
Reject if explanation contradicts the selected answer.
regeneration_hints: Reduce pointer complexity if the requested level is Easy.
Increase reasoning depth and distractor quality if the requested level is Hard.
Keep terminology consistent with introductory C teaching material.
